strengths: R2E provides a coherent contribution to biomedical NLP: representing candidate answers through retrieved, masked evidence enables passage-level Shapley attribution. Training with NULL evidence embeddings gives the attribution procedure a clearly defined missing-evidence baseline.

The results support the central claim that interpretability can coexist with competitive prediction. On Gene Description Facts, corrected R2E achieves MRR 0.260 versus 0.167 for MLM; on clinical outcomes, literature-only R2E achieves AUROC 0.632 versus 0.630. Using identical genetics evidence, R2E also improves over the ontology-based baseline, 0.579 versus 0.545.

Document-level temporal splits, training the encoder from scratch, component ablations, and experiments updating retrieval without retraining strengthen the empirical case. Detailed architectural specifications, hyperparameters, attribution pseudocode, and three released evaluation benchmarks support reimplementation of the core approach. Together, these establish a useful Findings-level contribution.
weaknesses: Exact experimental replication remains difficult. The training and retrieval corpus includes proprietary material, entity linking depends on undisclosed dictionaries and disambiguation components, and neither code nor model weights are released. The detailed appendices mitigate this limitation, but a reproducible public-corpus implementation would substantially strengthen confidence in the reported results.

The historical clinical-prediction claims need tighter qualification. Although literature is restricted to pre-2005 publications, no equivalent temporal filtering is described for the genetics evidence obtained from Minikel et al. (2024), and GPT-4 auditing can introduce later knowledge. These augmented results therefore do not establish strictly historical forecasting performance. Additionally, Appendix P uses development status as an efficacy proxy: discontinued phase II/III programmes are failures, while pre-registration and later stages count as successes.

Evidence of explanation usefulness is limited. Human validation covers only eight query-target pairs per task, annotated by one expert; the clinical examples were selected by familiarity. The clinical evidence-relevance AUROC of 0.665 against GPT-4 provides modest support for semantic relevance. Larger, independently annotated evaluations and comparison against similarity-guided auditing at the same annotation budget would better establish the benefit of Shapley-based explanations for expert decisions.

The comparisons do not fully isolate architectural gains. Much of the strongest ranking improvement accompanies frequency correction, but an equivalently corrected MLM baseline is absent even though Appendix G describes that correction. The small clinical auditing improvement also lacks a control establishing whether selecting evidence by Shapley value is more effective than simpler filtering strategies. These gaps limit the main-conference case without negating the demonstrated attribution capability.

Appendix F contains a local theoretical inconsistency: Section 3.4 samples negatives while excluding the true answer, whereas the derivation assumes query-independent uniform negatives. With N answers and positive conditional probability p, the stated sampling scheme gives optimal logit log((N-1)p/(1-p)); the independence assumption yielding log(Np) does not hold. The exact PMI interpretation in Appendix G consequently needs qualification, although the empirical correction results remain meaningful.
